flags: minor: distractors A, C, D all rely on extreme words (frequently/many, exactly/every, always), so the balanced key stands out by tone
R042-01.notes: Passage covers what pentimenti reveal (P2-3) and the preservation dilemma (P4-5). A misattributes, C overclaims, D contradicts 'No rule settles such disputes.'

R042-02.notes: P1: 'the covering had been added well after Vermeer's death.' C is wrong because X-rays decades earlier had already shown the Cupid. The key is a near-verbatim lift.

R042-03.notes: P1 is an anecdotal hook leading to pentimenti (P2) and the restoration debate (P4). B overstates the detail, C is the critics' view and not the author's argument, D is not in P1.

R042-04.notes: 'No rule settles such disputes' = resolves. Standard vocabulary-in-context item with sound distractors.

R042-05.notes: P3: a copyist who knows the final image has little reason to try alternatives, so the absence of changes could suggest a copy. B reverses the logic, C overreaches, and D is not supported. The hedged 'could be' fits the passage's 'sometimes.'

R042-06.notes: P2: 'infrared cameras can reveal sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied.' A is the X-ray detail from the same sentence, which makes it a good distractor.

R042-07.notes: The examples are followed by 'each shows that the composition we see was not the only one the artist considered.' B is wrong because the Dresden change was not the artist's, and those examples are general.

R042-08.notes: The critics stress that generations knew the plain wall and that it had become part of the painting's appeal, so its history should count. A is the opposing (intention) view. B and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: D (and to a lesser degree B) also show 'many moments' of the artist's own revisions; A is best only because it alone includes 'the choices of people who came later' as well as the artist's original choice. Consider tightening the stem (e.g., 'including the choices of people who came later') so the reason A wins is clearer
R042-09.notes: The P5 claim lists the artist's first ideas, second thoughts and final choices, 'and sometimes the choices of people who came later.' The Dresden Vermeer covers both the artist's layer and a later hand's overpaint, so it covers the full claim.

flags: minor: very direct near-verbatim lookup; key is the longest choice
R042-10.notes: P2: 'A few become visible to the naked eye as the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent with age.' This is factually accurate (oil paint becomes more transparent over time, as with The Old Guitarist).
